meta.topic: The missed warnings: Army radar net and Opana, Ward/Condor submarine contacts, the Information Center, and message traffic on both sides
meta.timeConvention: Hawaii local time (HST, UTC-10:30 in 1941) as HH:MM. Tokyo = HST + 19h30m. Washington EST = HST + 5h30m. GCT = HST + 10h30m.
meta.units: Positions decimal degrees WGS84 (west negative); bearings degrees true; radar ranges in statute miles as the 1941 operators reported them (1 mi = 1609.344 m); altitudes metres.
meta.researchLimits: Direct page fetches were blocked in this session (history.navy.mil, ibiblio.org, wikipedia.org all unreachable) and the web-search budget ran out before every item could be re-checked. Items marked 'verifiedThisSession': true were confirmed from search-result text; everything else rests on standard published accounts recalled from memory and carries a confidence rating to match.

radarStations.name: Opana (Opana Point / Opana Hill, above Kawela Bay near Kahuku Point)
radarStations.positionBasis: Wikipedia / National Register coordinates for the Opana Radar Site NHL (21d41m08sN 158d00m36sW). The set was mobile, so the exact parking spot of the trucks within the hilltop clearing is not recoverable; treat as +/-150 m.
radarStations.elevationNote: 532 ft per National Park Service; George Elliott's own account says 526 ft (160 m).
radarStations.equipment: SCR-270-B mobile long-range search radar (the former Schofield Barracks training set, moved to Opana on Thanksgiving Day, 27 Nov 1941). On site: two trucks and an antenna trailer.
radarStations.operatingHours: Scheduled 04:00-07:00. Came on the air about 04:15 (generator maintenance delay). Kept running after 07:00 for training because the breakfast truck was late; shut down about 07:40-07:45.
operators: Pvt Joseph L. Lockard (oscilloscope operator, the experienced man)
Pvt George E. Elliott Jr. (plotter; recently transferred from the Hawaiian Air Force, learning the scope)
plotted: 06:45, 06:48, 06:51 - marks on the plotting overlay for one or two aircraft far to the north (the Japanese cruiser floatplane scouts); phoned in to the Information Center and put on the master board.
07:02-07:39 - the first-wave formation, from 132-137 mi at about 3 deg east of north down to 20-22 mi (see opanaPlots).
After the crew returned later in the morning the set tracked aircraft withdrawing to the north (see note in infoCenter.events 10:02).
radarStations.note: The only station still radiating after 07:00. Sources disagree on first-contact range: Lockard told the Information Center 132 miles; Elliott's plot and testimony say 137; several accounts quote 136.

radarStations.name: Kawailoa (north shore uplands above Haleiwa/Waimea; also the camp where the Opana crew lived, 9 road miles from Opana)
radarStations.positionBasis: ESTIMATE ONLY: placed in the Kawailoa uplands consistent with the 9-road-mile distance to Opana. No surveyed 1941 site position was found. Uncertainty about +/-3 km.
radarStations.elevationNote: Unknown; 90 m is a terrain guess for the Kawailoa plateau, for rendering only.
radarStations.operatingHours: 04:00-07:00; shut down at 07:00; back on the air after the attack began.
plotted: 06:45 - target about 130-135 mi north of Oahu heading south (same contact as Opana and Kaaawa), phoned to the Information Center.
radarStations.note: First of the mobile sets deployed (order of deployment per the Signal Company history: Kawailoa, Waianae, Koko Head, Kaaawa, Fort Shafter).

radarStations.name: Kaaawa (windward coast)
radarStations.positionBasis: ESTIMATE ONLY: placed at Kaaawa village on the coastal strip. Exact 1941 site not found. Uncertainty about +/-2 km.
radarStations.elevationNote: Unknown; value is a guess for rendering only.
plotted: 06:45 - target about 130-135 mi north of Oahu heading south, phoned to the Information Center.

radarStations.name: Koko Head (south-east Oahu)
radarStations.positionBasis: ESTIMATE ONLY: placed on the Koko Head headland where a permanent radar station was later built. Exact 1941 truck position not found. Uncertainty about +/-1 km.
radarStations.elevationNote: Unknown; Koko Head summit is about 196 m. Rendering guess only.
plotted: About 06:13 - sightings south of the island (reported with Fort Shafter in Arakaki & Kuborn; routine traffic, not connected with the attack).
radarStations.note: The 06:13 item is recalled from Arakaki & Kuborn and was not re-verified this session.

radarStations.name: Fort Shafter (ridge behind the post)
radarStations.positionBasis: ESTIMATE ONLY: on the ridge immediately mauka (inland) of Fort Shafter. Exact site not found. Uncertainty about +/-1 km.
radarStations.operatingHours: CONFLICT: the National Park Service says only five mobile stations were active that morning and that the Fort Shafter set was not yet operating; Arakaki & Kuborn have Fort Shafter and Koko Head picking up targets south of Oahu about 06:13. If shown operating: 04:00-07:00.
plotted: About 06:13 - sightings south of the island (per Arakaki & Kuborn; conflicts with NPS statement that this set was not operating).
radarStations.note: Recommend rendering this station as present but 'status uncertain'.

radarStations.name: Waianae (leeward coast)
radarStations.positionBasis: ESTIMATE ONLY: placed at Waianae. Exact 1941 site not found. Uncertainty about +/-3 km.
radarStations.note: No record found of anything plotted by Waianae before 07:00.

radarNetwork.organisation: Aircraft Warning Service (AWS), Hawaiian Department, operated by the Signal Company, Aircraft Warning, Hawaii (Capt Wilfred H. Tetley), headquartered at Schofield Barracks; under the Department Signal Officer (Lt Col Carroll A. Powell), not yet turned over to the Hawaiian Interceptor Command (14th Pursuit Wing, Brig Gen Howard C. Davidson).
radarNetwork.sets: Six SCR-270-B mobile sets on Oahu: five deployed Aug-Sept 1941 (Kawailoa, Waianae, Koko Head, Kaaawa, Fort Shafter) plus the Schofield training set moved to Opana in late November. Three fixed SCR-271 sets (planned for Mount Kaala on Oahu, Haleakala on Maui and Kokee on Kauai) had been delivered but were not installed.
radarNetwork.hours: By General Short's order after the 27 November warning the sets operated 04:00-07:00 daily, the hours he judged most dangerous. On weekdays training continued 07:00-11:00 and maintenance in the afternoon; on Sundays the net closed at 07:00.
radarNetwork.limits: No identification (IFF), no height finding, no Navy or bomber liaison officers at the Information Center, no controller on duty; the system was officially still in training status.
radarNetwork.stationCountConflict: Sources give 'five mobile stations' (NPS; Army accounts of December 1941) and 'six' (Arakaki & Kuborn and others). The difference is the Fort Shafter set.

antenna.type: Broadside array of horizontal half-wave dipoles in front of a wire reflector screen (the 'bedspring'), one antenna for both transmit and receive
antenna.layout: 4 wide x 9 high on the Opana mobile set (some photographs and the later models show 4 wide x 8 high = 32)
antenna.dimensionBasis: ESTIMATE from wavelength: half-wave dipole at 106 MHz is 1.41 m; four end-to-end and nine rows at half-wave spacing. Not taken from a drawing.
antenna.overallHeightNote: 55 ft folding steel lattice mast derived from a well-drilling rig, carried on the trailer and raised to vertical; steadied by outriggers/guys.
antenna.rotation: Whole mast and array turn through 360 deg at about 1 rpm; the operator could stop it and inch it by hand control to hold on a target and read azimuth.
antenna.appearance: Tall, flat, open rectangular lattice of thin rods and wires, taller than wide, olive drab, on a slender lattice mast rising from a flat-bed trailer; no dish, no radome.

display.type: A-scope (range-amplitude oscilloscope). NOT a plan-position indicator: there was no map-like picture.
display.description: A single horizontal green trace on a 5-inch cathode-ray tube. The transmitter pulse shows as a tall spike at the left; an echo is a vertical 'pip' rising from the baseline, its distance along the trace giving range and its height and width giving a rough idea of size. Ground returns from nearby mountains fill the first 20 miles or so with permanent echoes.
display.rangeReadout: The operator turned a handwheel that slid the trace until the pip sat on a hairline, then read miles from a mechanical range dial (scale to 150 miles).
display.azimuthReadout: Read from the antenna azimuth scale with the array turned for maximum pip height; called to the plotter, who marked range and azimuth on a map overlay with a range arm centred on the station.
display.whatLockardSaw: At 07:02 a pip so large (the main-pulse-sized echo of 180+ aircraft) that Lockard first checked whether the set was faulty.
display.conflictNote: Some web sources describe a '12-inch PPI' for the SCR-270; that belongs to later equipment, not the 1941 SCR-270-B used at Opana.

performance.note: Frequency, pulse width, PRF, 100 kW peak power, 1 rpm rotation and roughly 150-mile range were confirmed from search results this session; accuracy figures are recalled and less certain.

vehicles.role: Operating van: receiver, oscilloscope, operator seat, plotting table and field telephones
Power truck carrying the PE-74 gasoline engine-generator
Flat trailer carrying the folding mast, turntable and antenna array
Tractor truck that towed the antenna trailer (may not have remained on site; NPS describes 'two trucks and a trailer' at Opana)

scr270.note: SCR-270 designed at the Signal Corps Laboratories (Fort Monmouth) and built by Westinghouse. The Opana set is commonly cited as serial number 012 (not re-verified this session). Normal crew was three (operator, plotter, motorman for the generator); only two men were on duty at Opana on 7 December.

opanaPlots.basis: Range 'approximately 135 miles north' per Arakaki & Kuborn (another document says 130). Azimuth recorded only as 'north'; 0 deg assumed. Position computed from Opana.
opanaPlots.note: Single aircraft (or two) heading south - the Chikuma/Tone reconnaissance floatplanes launched 05:30. Also seen by Kawailoa and Kaaawa. Phoned in and plotted at the Information Center.

opanaPlots.basis: Elliott's Army Pearl Harbor Board testimony refers to overlay marks at 6:45, 6:48 and 6:51; their ranges and azimuths were not recovered.
opanaPlots.note: Second mark on the early (scout plane) track.
Third mark on the early (scout plane) track.

opanaPlots.basis: Recorded range and azimuth; position computed from Opana on a great circle. Using 137 mi instead gives 23.6657, -157.8967.
opanaPlots.note: FIRST CONTACT with the first wave. Lockard reported 132 miles to the Information Center; Elliott plotted and testified 137; 136 appears in Lockard-derived accounts. Azimuth '3 degrees east of north' (Elliott on the phone: 'from the north, three points east'). 132 fits the later plots best (see trackModel).

opanaPlots.basis: Range from the NPS Opana page (07:06, 'large target 113 miles out'). Azimuth is MODEL (straight track), not recorded.
opanaPlots.note: Time is doubtful: 113 mi four minutes after 132-137 mi implies 285-360 mph. 113 mi fits about 07:08-07:10 at the 180 mph shown by the other plots. Use the trackModel for motion.

opanaPlots.basis: Range from NPS ('92 miles away, travelling at 180 mph'). Azimuth MODEL.
Range as given in Walter Lord, Day of Infamy (recalled; not re-verified this session). Azimuth MODEL.
Range as given in Walter Lord (recalled; some accounts say 45). Azimuth MODEL.
Time 07:39 from NPS; range 22 mi (Lord and others) or 20 mi (National Archives; Lockard). Azimuth MODEL.
opanaPlots.note: LAST PLOT. Echo lost in the permanent echoes / ground return from the surrounding mountains. Some sources round the time to 07:40.

opanaGeometry.azimuthReference: Assumed TRUE north. Sources say only '3 degrees east of north'; if the set had been oriented to magnetic north (declination about 11 deg E in 1941) the track would lie about 14 deg true, which does not fit a carrier force launching from due north of Oahu, so true is adopted.

trackModel.description: Constant-speed straight track for animation, fitted to the recorded plots: starts at the 07:02 fix (132 mi, 003 deg), flies course 182.3 deg true at 180 mph ground speed (156 kn) toward Kahuku Point. Reproduces 93 mi at 07:15 (recorded 92), 63 at 07:25 (62), 48 at 07:30 (47), 21 at 07:39 (20-22).
trackModel.basis: MODEL / own geometry, not a record. Points after 07:39 are extrapolation past loss of radar contact. Japanese records put Fuchida's deployment flare 'off Kahuku Point' at 07:40; the radar has the formation still about 20 miles north then, so the model reaches Kahuku Point near 07:45. Blend toward the flight-path data of the air-attack dataset if they differ.

infoCenter.name: Aircraft Warning Service Information Center, Fort Shafter (temporary frame building; a large table-map plotting board with a raised platform or balcony for the controller and pursuit officer - layout as generally described, no plan seen)
infoCenter.positionBasis: ESTIMATE ONLY: Fort Shafter cantonment near the headquarters area. The 1941 temporary building was not located on a plan this session. Uncertainty about +/-400 m.

people.name: 1st Lt Kermit A. Tyler
people.role: Pursuit officer on duty 04:00-08:00 (78th Pursuit Squadron, Wheeler Field). Second time in the Center, no training in the job, no orders beyond being there. The only officer present.

people.name: Pvt Joseph P. McDonald
people.role: Switchboard operator, Signal Company Aircraft Warning; took Opana's call on the administrative line

people.name: Plotters (about seven or eight enlisted men) and the 'historian' recorder
people.role: Manned the plotting table 04:00-07:00; left for breakfast at 07:00

people.name: Pvt Richard Schimmel
people.role: Off-duty friend of McDonald in the tents beside the Center; later accounts say he copied down McDonald's note of the Opana message

people.name: Maj Kenneth P. Bergquist
people.role: 14th Pursuit Wing operations officer who had been building the Center; not present until after the attack began

people.name: Maj Lorry N. Tindal
people.role: Controller; not present 07:00-08:00, arrived after the attack began and took over

events.event: Stations open; plotters man the board; Lt Tyler begins his 04:00-08:00 watch as pursuit officer.
First plots of the morning appear on the board (Tyler's recollection: about 06:10; Arakaki & Kuborn: Koko Head and Fort Shafter sightings south of Oahu about 06:13).
Kaaawa, Opana and Kawailoa each phone in a target about 130-135 miles north of Oahu heading south; it is placed on the master plotting board. Nobody acts on it.
Scheduled operating period ends. Plotters and recorder leave for breakfast; five stations shut down. Only Tyler and switchboard operator McDonald remain.
Opana detects the first wave (132-137 miles, 3 deg east of north).

Elliott tries the direct tactical line to the plotters - no one answers - then rings the administrative line and reaches McDonald: 'Large number of planes coming in from the north, three points east.' (NPS gives 07:06 for this call; other accounts 07:09-07:10.) McDonald says there is nobody there; Elliott asks him to find someone.
McDonald, having written the message down and timed it by the Center clock, takes it to Tyler at the plotting table. Tyler is not concerned. McDonald rings Opana back.

Lockard, now on the line, insists it is the biggest flight he has ever seen. Tyler takes the phone, listens, and says: 'Well, don't worry about it.' He assumes it is the flight of B-17s due from California (he had heard KGMB playing Hawaiian music through the night, which a bomber-pilot friend had told him meant a mainland flight was homing in) or possibly Navy carrier planes. He cannot say so on an open line. McDonald asks whether to recall the plotters or tell Wheeler Field; Tyler again says not to worry.
Opana loses the echo at 20-22 miles. No further report is made.
Attack begins. Tyler steps outside shortly afterwards, sees aircraft and smoke over Pearl Harbor and at first takes it for Navy practice.
A telephone call (from Wheeler Field) tells Tyler there is an attack; he recalls the Signal Corps plotters. Maj Tindal arrives about 08:20 and takes over as controller; Maj Bergquist follows.
Radar stations progressively back on the air during the next half hour.

Between about 10:02 and 10:39 the radar plots show aircraft withdrawing northward from Oahu. The information is not exploited; the Navy, misled by a reciprocal radio-direction-finder bearing, searches to the south and south-west. The Opana inbound track does not reach the Navy for two days.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: 1.75 nautical miles south-west of the Pearl Harbor entrance buoys (as worded in the Joint Committee report), with the entrance buoys taken at about 21.2933, -157.9600. Other texts say the periscope was about 1,000 yards seaward of the buoys. Uncertainty +/-1.5 km.
seaContacts.event: Minesweeper USS Condor (AMc-14), sweeping with USS Crossbill off the entrance, sights a periscope close aboard off her port bow in the darkness (about 50 yards in most accounts; the official narrative says about 100 feet and on a collision course), in an area where US submarines were forbidden to run submerged. The object turns sharply away to port. Sighted by the officer of the deck, Ensign R. C. McCloy, and confirmed by the quartermaster at the wheel (Uttrick).

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: vicinity of the 03:42 sighting.
seaContacts.event: Condor signals USS Ward by yardarm blinker light (sources give times between 03:50 and 03:58; 03:57 is the usual figure).
seaContacts.message: Sighted submerged submarine on westerly course, speed 9 knots.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: Ward's patrol station was a two-mile square off the entrance buoys.
seaContacts.event: USS Ward (DD-139; Lt William W. Outerbridge, in command since 5 December and on his first patrol as captain) goes to general quarters and searches with sonar for about an hour, to the west - the wrong direction. Nothing found; secures from general quarters about 04:35-04:45. No report is made to shore.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: anti-torpedo net across the entrance channel abreast Bishop's Point.
seaContacts.event: Anti-torpedo net gate opened for the returning minesweepers. Crossbill passes in about 05:08, Condor about 05:32. Because the tug Keosanqua is due out about 06:15 to meet Antares, the gate is left open.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE as above.
seaContacts.event: Ward and Condor talk by voice radio (05:20-05:36). Outerbridge realises he has searched in the wrong direction. Bishop's Point naval radio station hears and logs the exchange but does not pass it on.
seaContacts.message: Ward: 'What was the approximate distance and course of the submarine that you sighted?' Condor: 'The course was about what we were steering at the time, 020 magnetic, and about 1,000 yards from the entrance, apparently heading for the entrance.' ... Ward: 'When was the last time approximately that you saw the submarine?' Condor: 'Approximately 0350 and he was apparently heading for the entrance.'
seaContacts.messageNote: Wording as printed from the Bishop's Point radio log (Joint Committee Exhibit); recalled, not re-verified word for word this session. A paraphrase 'Sub's course was 020 magnetic and was heading for entrance buoys' was confirmed.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: Antares approaching the entrance from the south-west, a mile or two off the buoys.
seaContacts.event: Stores ship USS Antares (AKS-3; Cdr Lawrence C. Grannis), arriving from Canton and Palmyra with a 500-ton steel barge in tow and waiting for the tug Keosanqua, sights a suspicious object about 1,500 yards on her starboard quarter - a small conning tower, awash, apparently following her toward the harbour. She notifies Ward by visual signal.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: over the submarine.
seaContacts.event: PBY-5 14-P-1 of VP-14 (Ensign William P. Tanner), on the dawn security patrol from Kaneohe, sees the object and drops two smoke pots to mark it for Ward. (A Marine Corps Base Hawaii history gives 06:50 for the PBY's sighting.)

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE.
seaContacts.event: Ward's officer of the deck, Lt (jg) Oscar W. Goepner, calls: 'Captain, come on the bridge.' Conning tower with periscope visible astern of Antares, making 8-10 knots. Described as a cylindrical tube about 80 feet long with a small oval conning tower, no deck, painted dark green.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE.
seaContacts.event: General quarters; Ward accelerates from 5 to 25 knots and bears down on the submarine.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE, +/-3 km: the text of Ward's 13 December action report gives no latitude/longitude, only that the submarine sank in 1,200 feet of water in the defensive sea area off the entrance (her logged position was not retrieved this session; the wreck is said to lie about 1.5 miles from where Ward reported the sinking). The wreck was found on 28 August 2002 by the Hawaii Undersea Research Laboratory in about 400 m (1,300 ft), three to five miles off the harbour mouth; its exact position is withheld by the US government. The point given is on the 400 m contour about four nautical miles south of the harbour mouth.
seaContacts.event: FIRST AMERICAN SHOTS OF THE PACIFIC WAR. Ward opens fire with two of her four 4-inch/50 guns, one round each. No. 1 gun (forecastle) fires at about 100 yards and the shell passes over the conning tower. No. 3 gun (starboard waist, on the galley deckhouse) fires at 50 yards or less and hits at the waterline at the junction of hull and conning tower; the submarine heels to starboard, slows and sinks. It passes close under Ward's stern into four depth charges set for 100 feet, rolled on whistle signals. A large oil slick appears. The PBY then drops depth bombs on the spot.

weapons.guns: 4-inch/50 calibre Mark 9, No. 1 and No. 3 mounts, one round each

seaContacts.note: The NHHC transcription of the action report reads 'at a range of 560 yards or less' for No. 3 gun in one paragraph but '50 yards or less' in another; 50 yards is consistent with the rest of the report. The 2002 wreck shows a 4-inch hole at the base of the conning tower on the starboard side. Which midget this was (from I-20 or I-22) is disputed.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE.
seaContacts.event: Ward sights a motor sampan inside the restricted area and runs it down; its crew show a white flag. A Coast Guard cutter later takes it to Honolulu.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE.
seaContacts.event: Outerbridge's first voice-radio report to Commandant, Fourteenth Naval District (via Bishop's Point radio).
seaContacts.message: We have dropped depth charges upon subs operating in defensive sea area.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE.
seaContacts.event: Reflecting that the first message could be read as just another doubtful sonar contact, Outerbridge sends a second to make clear he has seen and shot at a surfaced submarine. It is followed by 'Stand by for further messages.'
seaContacts.message: We have attacked, fired upon, and dropped depth charges upon submarine operating in defensive sea area.
seaContacts.messageNote: Ward's own written report of 13 December gives the time as 06:45 and the words '...on a submarine operating in defensive sea areas.' The 06:51/06:53 times and wording above are those of the radio log used by the Joint Committee.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: same spot as Ward's attack.
seaContacts.event: PBY 14-P-1 reports its own attack in code to Patrol Wing Two. Decoding and a request for verification consume about half an hour.
seaContacts.message: Sunk one enemy submarine one mile south of Pearl Harbor.
seaContacts.messageNote: Variously printed as 'Sank enemy submarine one mile south Pearl Harbor' / 'Sunk one enemy sub 1 mile south of Pearl Harbor'.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE.
seaContacts.event: Ward gains a sonar contact on what she takes to be another submarine and at 07:05 drops more depth charges (five in most accounts); at 07:06 a black oil bubble is seen 300 yards astern.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: Fourteenth Naval District headquarters, Pearl Harbor Navy Yard. Approximate only.
seaContacts.event: After a decoding delay Ward's 06:53 message reaches the district watch officer, Lt Cdr Harold Kaminski USNR. He cannot raise the Commandant's aide, telephones the chief of staff, Capt John B. Earle, tells the CINCPAC duty staff, and on his own initiative orders the ready-duty destroyer Monaghan out.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE as above.
seaContacts.event: Earle telephones Rear Adm Claude C. Bloch (Commandant, 14th Naval District). After many false submarine reports in the past months they decide, since Ward will presumably amplify and Monaghan is going out, to 'await further developments'.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: CINCPAC headquarters at the Submarine Base. Approximate only.
seaContacts.event: Lt Cdr Francis L. Black, assistant fleet duty officer, relays Kaminski's report to the fleet duty officer, Cdr Vincent R. Murphy, who is dressing at his quarters. Murphy tries to ring Kaminski for details (line busy) and goes to the office.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: Patrol Wing Two command centre, Naval Air Station Ford Island. Approximate only.
seaContacts.event: The decoded PBY message reaches Lt Cdr Logan C. Ramsey, Patrol Wing Two operations officer. Suspecting a mistake he asks for authentication, then begins drafting a search plan and at about 07:40 telephones the CINCPAC duty officer.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE as above.
seaContacts.event: Murphy telephones Admiral Husband E. Kimmel at his quarters on Makalapa hill with the Ward report. Kimmel: 'I'll be right down.' He is waiting for confirmation and still on the telephone with Murphy about the sampan report when the attack begins at 07:55; a yeoman breaks in to say the signal tower reports Japanese planes attacking and that it is no drill.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: Monaghan in the destroyer nest in East Loch north-east of Ford Island; take the berth from the ship-positions dataset.
seaContacts.event: Ready-duty destroyer USS Monaghan (DD-354; Lt Cdr William P. Burford) receives the order to go out.
seaContacts.message: Proceed immediately and contact Ward in defensive sea area.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: main channel at the turn into West Loch.
seaContacts.event: USS Helm (DD-388; Lt Cdr Chester E. Carroll), the only ship under way in the harbour, is turning into West Loch for the deperming buoys when the attack begins. She reverses course and heads for the sea at 25-27 knots.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: net gate abreast Bishop's Point.
seaContacts.event: Helm passes the gate vessel outbound.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: Tripod Reef on the west (right-hand, outbound) side of the entrance channel, north of buoy No. 1.
seaContacts.event: Helm sights the conning tower of a submarine to the right of the channel, northward of buoy No. 1. At 08:20 she opens fire on it off Tripod Reef; no hits seen; the submarine, apparently touching bottom on the ledge of the reef in the line of breakers, slides off and submerges. (This is Ensign Kazuo Sakamaki's Ha-19, which later drifts ashore off Bellows Field.)
seaContacts.message: Small Jap sub trying to penetrate channel.
seaContacts.messageNote: Wording as given in Walter Lord; recalled, not re-verified this session.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE as above.
seaContacts.event: Monaghan under way (08:27 by her own report; CINCPAC's report says 08:30, 'temporarily delayed by the initiation of the enemy action'), heading down the north channel west of Ford Island.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: channel north-west of Ford Island.
seaContacts.event: Seaplane tender Curtiss is flying the signal for a submarine sighted and firing at a conning tower about 700 yards off her starboard quarter; minelayer-tender Medusa is firing too. Monaghan sees the midget about 1,000 yards ahead, rings up flank speed and steers to ram. The midget fires one torpedo at Curtiss (misses, explodes against a dock at Pearl City) and one at Monaghan (misses, explodes on the Ford Island shore).

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE: between Curtiss's berth off Pearl City and the north-west shore of Ford Island. Uncertainty +/-300 m; reconcile with the ship-positions dataset.
seaContacts.event: Monaghan rams the midget submarine a glancing blow and at 08:44 drops two depth charges that explode 50-100 yards astern, lifting her stern. The midget is destroyed. Monaghan, unable to stop, runs into a burning derrick barge at Beckoning Point, backs clear and proceeds to sea.

seaContacts.positionBasis: ESTIMATE as above.
seaContacts.event: Anti-torpedo net gate finally closed - it had stood open since 04:58, nearly four hours. (The same official narrative also says it was 'not closed until after 0800 when ordered closed by Headquarters'.)

messages.text: Henceforth, we would like to have you make reports concerning vessels along the following lines insofar as possible: 1. The waters (of Pearl Harbor) are to be divided roughly into five sub-areas ... Area A. Waters between Ford Island and the Arsenal. Area B. Waters adjacent to the Island south and west of Ford Island. Area C. East Loch. Area D. Middle Loch. Area E. West Loch and the communicating water routes. 2. With regard to warships and aircraft carriers, we would like to have you report on those at anchor (these are not so important), tied up at wharves, buoys and in docks ...
messages.note: The 'bomb plot' message, Tokyo No. 83. Intercepted and translated in Washington on 9 October 1941; never sent to Kimmel or Short. Text abridged.

messages.from: Chief of Naval Operations (Adm Harold R. Stark)
messages.text: This despatch is to be considered a war warning. Negotiations with Japan looking toward stabilization of conditions in the Pacific have ceased and an aggressive move by Japan is expected within the next few days. The number and equipment of Japanese troops and the organization of naval task forces indicates an amphibious expedition against either the Philippines, Thai or Kra Peninsula or possibly Borneo. Execute an appropriate defensive deployment preparatory to carrying out the tasks assigned in WPL 46. Inform district and Army authorities. A similar warning is being sent by War Department. SPENAVO inform British. Continental districts Guam Samoa directed take appropriate measures against sabotage.
messages.note: The 'war warning'. Date-time group 272337 (GCT), i.e. 13:07 Hawaii time on 27 November, is the time of origin; Kimmel saw it that afternoon. Hawaii is not named among the likely targets.

messages.to: Commanding General, Hawaiian Department (Lt Gen Walter C. Short)
messages.text: Negotiations with Japan appear to be terminated to all practical purposes with only the barest possibilities that the Japanese Government might come back and offer to continue. Japanese future action unpredictable but hostile action possible at any moment. If hostilities cannot, repeat cannot, be avoided the United States desires that Japan commit the first overt act. This policy should not, repeat not, be construed as restricting you to a course of action that might jeopardize your defense. Prior to hostile Japanese action you are directed to undertake such reconnaissance and other measures as you deem necessary but these measures should be carried out so as not, repeat not, to alarm civil population or disclose intent. Report measures taken. Should hostilities occur you will carry out the tasks assigned in Rainbow Five so far as they pertain to Japan. Limit dissemination of this highly secret information to minimum essential officers.
messages.note: Received at Fort Shafter on the afternoon of 27 November. Short chose Alert No. 1 (sabotage) within the hour.

messages.text: Report Department alerted to prevent sabotage. Liaison with Navy REURAD four seven two twenty seventh.
messages.note: Short's reply. Nobody in Washington queried it, and Short took the silence as approval.

messages.from: Commander in Chief Combined Fleet (Adm Isoroku Yamamoto), flagship Nagato, Hashirajima
messages.to: Combined Fleet, including the Kido Butai at sea
messages.text: Niitakayama nobore 1208 (Climb Mount Niitaka 1208)
messages.note: Sent 17:30 Tokyo time on 2 December 1941 = 22:00 on 1 December Hawaii time. Pre-arranged phrase meaning hostilities will open on 8 December (Tokyo date). Mount Niitaka (Yu Shan, Taiwan) was then the highest peak in the Japanese empire.

messages.text: In view of the present situation, the presence in port of warships, airplane carriers, and cruisers is of utmost importance. Hereafter, to the utmost of your ability, let me know day by day. Wire me in each case whether or not there are any observation balloons above Pearl Harbor or if there are any indications that they will be sent up. Also advise me whether or not the warships are provided with anti-mine nets.
messages.note: Tokyo No. 123. Intercepted but not translated by the US Army until 30 December 1941.

messages.text: [Parts 1-13 of the fourteen-part memorandum, Tokyo No. 902, replying to the US note of 26 November.]
messages.note: Intercepted, decrypted (Purple) and delivered to President Roosevelt about 21:30 EST on 6 December = 16:00 Hawaii time. Roosevelt to Harry Hopkins: 'This means war.' Nothing was sent to Hawaii.

messages.from: Japanese Consulate General, Honolulu (Consul General Nagao Kita; drafted by Takeo Yoshikawa, alias Vice-Consul Tadashi Morimura)
messages.text: ... At the present time there are no signs of barrage balloon equipment ... In my opinion the battleships do not have torpedo nets ... I imagine that in all probability there is considerable opportunity left to take advantage for a surprise attack against these places.
messages.note: Honolulu No. 253, 6 December. Excerpts; not translated in Washington until 8 December.

messages.from: Japanese Consulate General, Honolulu (Kita; drafted by Takeo Yoshikawa)
messages.text: 1. On the evening of the 5th, among the battleships which entered port were [garbled] and one submarine tender. The following ships were observed at anchor on the 6th: 9 battleships, 3 light cruisers, 3 submarine tenders, 17 destroyers, and in addition there were 4 light cruisers, 2 destroyers lying at docks (the heavy cruisers and airplane carriers have all left). 2. It appears that no air reconnaissance is being conducted by the fleet air arm.
messages.note: Honolulu No. 254 - THE LAST SHIP-LOCATION REPORT. Filed by commercial cable (RCA) on the evening of 6 December; the 18:00 hour is approximate. Tokyo relayed its substance to the Kido Butai that night ('...all carriers and heavy cruisers are at sea... Oahu is quiet'). Intercepted by the US but not translated until 8 December. The opening of the text was confirmed from search results this session; the remainder is recalled from the hearing exhibits.

messages.text: The Japanese Government regrets to have to notify hereby the American Government that in view of the attitude of the American Government it cannot but consider that it is impossible to reach an agreement through further negotiations.
messages.note: Closing sentence of Part 14. Intercepted by the Navy's Bainbridge Island station about 03:05 EST on 7 December (21:35 on the 6th Hawaii time); in American hands in English by about 08:00 EST. Intercept time recalled, not re-verified.

messages.text: Will the Ambassador please submit to the United States Government (if possible to the Secretary of State) our reply to the United States at 1:00 p.m. on the 7th, your time.
messages.note: Tokyo No. 907, the 'one o'clock' delivery message. Intercepted 04:37 EST 7 December (23:07 on the 6th Hawaii time), translated by about 09:00-10:20 EST. 1:00 p.m. in Washington was 07:30 a.m. at Pearl Harbor - about dawn. Col Rufus Bratton and Lt Cdr Alwin Kramer both saw the significance. A companion message (No. 910) ordered the embassy to destroy its remaining cipher machine and codes. Bratton and Brig Gen Sherman Miles reached Marshall with it at 11:25 EST (05:55 Hawaii time).

messages.text: Sighted submerged submarine on westerly course, speed 9 knots.
messages.note: See seaContacts 03:57.

messages.from: Chief of Staff, US Army (Gen George C. Marshall), War Department message No. 529
messages.to: Commanding General, Hawaiian Department (also to Manila, Panama, San Francisco)
messages.text: Japanese are presenting at one p.m. Eastern Standard Time today what amounts to an ultimatum also they are under orders to destroy their code machine immediately. Just what significance the hour set may have we do not know but be on alert accordingly. Inform naval authorities of this communication. Marshall.
messages.note: Drafted about 11:50 EST, filed at the War Department Signal Center 12:00-12:01 EST (06:30 Hawaii time). Army radio could not raise Honolulu because of atmospheric conditions, so Col Edward F. French sent it by Western Union at 12:17 EST (06:47 Hawaii time) to San Francisco for relay by RCA. Marshall did not use the scrambler telephone and declined Stark's offer of Navy radio.

messages.from: USS Ward (Lt W. W. Outerbridge), voice radio
messages.text: We have dropped depth charges upon subs operating in defensive sea area.
messages.note: First report.

messages.from: USS Ward (Lt W. W. Outerbridge), voice radio
messages.text: We have attacked, fired upon, and dropped depth charges upon submarine operating in defensive sea area.
messages.note: Second, stronger report, followed by 'Stand by for further messages.' Reached the district duty officer about 07:12 after decoding.

messages.to: Commander Patrol Wing Two / Commander Task Force Three
messages.text: Sunk one enemy submarine one mile south of Pearl Harbor.
messages.note: Coded; decoded at Ford Island about 07:30-07:35. Wording varies between sources.

messages.to: Information Center, Fort Shafter (Pvt Joseph McDonald)
messages.text: Large number of planes coming in from the north, three points east.
messages.note: Time 07:06 per NPS; other accounts about 07:10. 'Three points east' = three degrees east of north.

messages.text: Well, don't worry about it.
messages.note: Tyler's own words as he gave them to the Roberts Commission, which also fixes the time at about 07:20. Often quoted as 'Don't worry about it.'

messages.to: RCA office, 223 South King Street, Honolulu
messages.text: [Marshall's message No. 529, in code, addressed to the Commanding General, Fort Shafter; not marked priority.]
messages.note: Received in Honolulu 22 minutes before the first bombs. The teletype link to Fort Shafter was not working that early on a Sunday, so the envelope went into the pigeonhole for the Kalihi district and was taken out by motorcycle messenger Tadao Fuchikami along with his other telegrams. He was caught in traffic and stopped at roadblocks during the raid.

messages.text: Enemy fleet not in Lahaina anchorage.
messages.note: 03:05 Tokyo time. Launched 05:30 Hawaii time. One reference work claims this aircraft's radio failed; Prange and Japanese records have the report received.

messages.to: Kido Butai and the approaching first wave
messages.text: Enemy formation at anchor; nine battleships, one heavy cruiser, six light cruisers are in the harbor. ... Wind direction from 80 degrees, speed 14 meters, clearance over enemy fleet 1,700 meters, cloud density seven.
messages.note: About 03:05-03:08 Tokyo time. This is the aircraft whose approach the three northern radar stations plotted from 06:45. Wording per Prange; recalled, not re-verified.

messages.from: Cdr Mitsuo Fuchida (first-wave leader, Akagi B5N2)
messages.text: [Signal pistol: one 'black dragon' flare = surprise achieved, torpedo planes attack first. Thinking the fighters had not seen it, Fuchida fired a second; the dive-bomber leader read two flares as 'surprise lost' and attacked at once.]
messages.note: 03:10 Tokyo time, north of Kahuku Point.

messages.from: Cdr Mitsuo Fuchida (radioman PO1c Norinobu Mizuki)
messages.text: To, To, To
messages.note: 03:19 Tokyo time. First syllable of totsugeki seyo - 'charge' / all forces attack. Sent off the north-west coast near Waimea Bay.

messages.text: Proceed immediately and contact Ward in defensive sea area.

messages.from: Cdr Mitsuo Fuchida (radioman PO1c Norinobu Mizuki)
messages.to: Vice Adm Nagumo (Akagi); heard also aboard Nagato in Japan
messages.text: Tora, Tora, Tora
messages.note: 03:23 Tokyo time. 'Tiger' - code for 'we have succeeded in surprise attack'.

messages.from: Lt Cdr Logan C. Ramsey, operations officer, Patrol Wing Two, Ford Island (broadcast in plain language on all frequencies)
messages.text: AIR RAID, PEARL HARBOR. THIS IS NOT DRILL.
messages.note: Ramsey saw a dive-bomber pull out over the Ford Island seaplane ramp at about 07:57, took it for a reckless American pilot until the bomb exploded, and ran across the hall to the radio room. Some printings read 'THIS IS NO DRILL'.

messages.from: CINCPAC (sent by the duty staff under Cdr Vincent Murphy)
messages.to: CINCLANT, CINCAF, OPNAV; rebroadcast to all ships present Hawaiian area
messages.text: AIR RAID ON PEARL HARBOR X THIS IS NOT DRILL
messages.note: Date-time group 071830 GCT = 08:00 Hawaii time. The surviving naval dispatch form reads 'AIRRAID ON PEARLHARBOR X THIS IS NOT DRILL'; the National Archives caption renders it 'THIS IS NO DRILL'.

messages.text: Small Jap sub trying to penetrate channel.
messages.note: Wording per Walter Lord; not re-verified.

messages.from: Ambassadors Kichisaburo Nomura and Saburo Kurusu
messages.to: Secretary of State Cordell Hull, Washington
messages.text: [Hand over the fourteen-part memorandum.]
messages.note: 14:20 EST - one hour twenty minutes after the 1:00 p.m. deadline and fifty-five minutes after the attack began (13:25 EST), because the embassy was slow to decode and type it.

messages.text: [Marshall's message No. 529 delivered, still in code.]
messages.note: Four hours and twelve minutes after it reached Honolulu.

messages.text: [Marshall's message decoded and delivered.]
messages.note: Seven hours after the attack began. Short sent a copy to Kimmel, who threw it in the wastebasket.

army.alert: Alert No. 1 - defence against sabotage and uprisings within the islands, with no threat from without
army.orderedBy: Lt Gen Walter C. Short, Commanding General, Hawaiian Department
army.scale: Short's Standing Operating Procedure of 5 November 1941: No. 1 = sabotage; No. 2 = No. 1 plus defence against air, surface and submarine attack; No. 3 = full defence against all-out attack.
consequences: Aircraft at Hickam, Wheeler and Bellows taken out of dispersal and parked close together, wingtip to wingtip, on the aprons so they could be guarded; guns unloaded and ammunition stored.
Pursuit squadrons on four hours' notice.
Anti-aircraft batteries mostly not in field positions; ammunition for mobile guns boxed in depots (Aliamanu Crater and elsewhere).
army.changed: Alert No. 3 ordered about 08:10 on 7 December, after the attack had begun.

navy.status: Fleet in port for the weekend under normal peacetime in-port routine (Condition 3: a fraction of anti-aircraft guns manned, ammunition in ready boxes, many locked). No anti-torpedo nets around the battleships, no barrage balloons.
navy.reconnaissance: No distant air search. Dawn security patrol only: three VP-14 PBYs from Kaneohe (including 14-P-1) over the fleet operating areas, plus four from Ford Island exercising with submarines.
navy.commander: Adm Husband E. Kimmel, Commander in Chief Pacific Fleet
navy.carriersAbsent: Enterprise (returning from Wake), Lexington (bound for Midway), Saratoga (San Diego).

alertStatus.commanders: Kimmel and Short had a golf date for Sunday morning. Kimmel was at his quarters on Makalapa; Short at his quarters at Fort Shafter.

espionage.agent: Ensign Takeo Yoshikawa, Imperial Japanese Navy intelligence, at the Honolulu consulate from 27 March 1941 under the name Tadashi Morimura (chancellor/vice-consul)

consulate.name: Japanese Consulate General, 1742 Nuuanu Avenue, Honolulu (Consul General Nagao Kita)

observationPoints.name: Shuncho-ro teahouse, Alewa Heights (now Natsunoya Tea House) - second-floor view over Pearl Harbor and Hickam, with a telescope
Aiea Heights and the Pearl City peninsula landing

espionage.method: Visual observation from public places, taxis and sightseeing flights; reports cabled in the diplomatic J-19 / PA-K2 systems over commercial circuits (RCA, Mackay).
espionage.lastReport: Honolulu No. 254, evening of 6 December (see messages).

timeline.event: Tokyo's 'bomb plot' message asks the Honolulu consulate to report ships by berthing area.
Navy 'war warning' originated in Washington; Army message No. 472 the same afternoon. Short orders Alert No. 1 (sabotage) and radar hours of 04:00-07:00.
Thanksgiving Day: the Schofield training SCR-270-B is moved to Opana.
'Climb Mount Niitaka 1208' transmitted (17:30 on 2 December, Tokyo).
Roosevelt reads the first 13 parts of the Japanese memorandum in Washington: 'This means war.'
Yoshikawa's last ship-location report (No. 254) cabled from Honolulu (hour approximate).
The 'deliver at 1:00 p.m.' message intercepted (04:37 EST, 7 December).
USS Condor sights a periscope off the Pearl Harbor entrance.
Condor to Ward by blinker: 'Sighted submerged submarine on westerly course, speed 9 knots.'
Army radar stations begin the morning watch (Opana about 04:15). Lt Tyler on duty at the Information Center.
Ward at general quarters, searching; nothing found.
Anti-torpedo net gate opened; left open after the minesweepers enter (05:08 and 05:32).
Ward-Condor radio exchange; overheard at Bishop's Point, not reported.
Cruisers Tone and Chikuma catapult reconnaissance floatplanes toward Lahaina and Pearl Harbor.
Washington (11:25 EST): Marshall reads the fourteen-part message and the 1:00 p.m. instruction.
Antares sights a midget submarine following her; Marshall's warning is filed in Washington (12:00 EST).
Ward sights the conning tower.
Ward opens fire and sinks the midget submarine. At the same minute Opana, Kawailoa and Kaaawa plot an aircraft about 130-135 miles north.
Marshall's warning leaves Washington by Western Union (12:17 EST).
Ward: 'We have dropped depth charges upon subs operating in defensive sea area.'
Ward: 'We have attacked, fired upon, and dropped depth charges upon submarine operating in defensive sea area.'
Radar watch ends; five stations close; plotters leave the Information Center. PBY 14-P-1 reports sinking a submarine.
Opana picks up the first wave: 132-137 miles, 3 degrees east of north.
Elliott telephones the Information Center (time approximate).
Ward's message reaches Lt Cdr Kaminski at 14th Naval District; he calls Capt Earle.
Earle calls Admiral Bloch; they decide to await further developments. Opana: target at 92 miles.
Tyler to Lockard: 'Well, don't worry about it.'
Opana: 62 miles. CINCPAC duty officer Murphy told of the Ward report.
Opana: 47 miles. 1:00 p.m. in Washington - the delivery deadline.
Marshall's warning arrives at RCA Honolulu.
Chikuma's scout reports the fleet in harbour; Tone's reports Lahaina empty.
Opana loses the echo at 20-22 miles.
Fuchida fires the deployment flare. Murphy telephones Kimmel. Ramsey telephones Murphy about the PBY report.
Lockard and Elliott shut down and leave by truck for breakfast at Kawailoa (time approximate).
'To, To, To' - attack.
Monaghan ordered to 'proceed immediately and contact Ward'.
'Tora, Tora, Tora' - surprise achieved.
First bombs. Helm, the only ship under way, turns for the sea.
Ramsey: 'AIR RAID, PEARL HARBOR. THIS IS NOT DRILL.'
CINCPAC: 'AIR RAID ON PEARL HARBOR X THIS IS NOT DRILL'.
Short orders Alert No. 3 (time approximate).
Helm sights a midget submarine on Tripod Reef; fires at 08:20.
Monaghan under way.
Monaghan rams and depth-charges a midget submarine north-west of Ford Island.
Net gate closed.
Washington (14:20 EST): Nomura and Kurusu hand Hull the memorandum.
Radar plots aircraft withdrawing north (to about 10:39); not acted on.
Fuchikami delivers Marshall's telegram to the Fort Shafter signal office.
Marshall's warning, decoded, reaches General Short's headquarters.
